The Platonic Solids. Five three-dimensional geometric shapes in which all faces are identical regular polygons, all edges are equal, and all angles are equal have been named after the ancient Greek philosopher Plato. These solids have fascinated mathematicians and natural philosophers since antiquity and represent the only possible configurations satisfying these symmetry constraints. They appear throughout nature in crystal structures, viral particles, and atomic geometry, and have inspired artistic and mystical interpretations for thousands of years.

The Tetrahedron has four equilateral triangular faces, four vertices, and six edges, making it the simplest Platonic solid and traditionally associated with fire. The Cube, or Hexahedron, has six square faces, eight vertices, and twelve edges, and is the most familiar solid, associated with earth. The Octahedron has eight equilateral triangular faces, six vertices, and twelve edges, symmetrical like two square pyramids base-to-base, and associated with air. The Dodecahedron has twelve regular pentagonal faces, twenty vertices, and thirty edges, and is the most complex, associated with the cosmos or universe as a whole. The Icosahedron has twenty equilateral triangular faces, twelve vertices, and thirty edges, and is associated with water.

Euclid proved these are the only five regular polyhedra, with no sixth existing, making them a complete and finite set. They were known to ancient Greek mathematicians and appear in Pythagorean and Platonic cosmology, though modern crystallography and chemistry confirm their deep mathematical necessity.
